title: Users Don't Care About Your Figma File
intro: A licence renewal site looked modern and didn't work: “Submit” clicked three times with no response. Calabro's point: first make things that work, and only then make them look appealing.

topics.title: Users Don't Care About Your Figma File

learn.title: Lack of clarity
learn.text:
Teams believe that if an interface looks clean, users will know how it works. Common problems:

• Unlabeled icons users must memorise
• Tooltips in place of labels or visible guidance
• Weak signifiers: buttons that look like plain text
• No defaults, even when the system knows the likely choice

Example: a signup form that showed password rules only **after** submission failed.

try.q: Password rules appear only after the form fails. Which problem is this?
options: Guidance hidden instead of visible
A destructive action placed beside a routine one
A click target that is too small
A modal that blocks the context
try.explain: Lack of clarity: rules were hidden when users needed them.

learn.title: Interaction and communication
learn.text:
**Interaction doubts:** tiny click targets, buttons that don't respond visually, decoration that looks clickable.

**Communication failures:** no confirmation after submit, progress indicators that appear too late, vague errors like “Try again later.”

When feedback is missing, people stop trusting the interface and fall back on screenshots and refreshes.

try.q: Submitting a form just refreshes the screen. What do users do next?
options: Stop trusting it and use workarounds
Assume it worked and move on
Read the documentation for help
Wait patiently for an email confirmation to arrive
try.explain: In his example, users had no way of knowing whether the request went through.

learn.title: Memory and bad neighbours
learn.text:
**Cognitive overload:** modals that hide the context users need, re-entering information, rules to remember across steps.

**Bad neighbours:** destructive actions beside save or confirm, styled alike, where muscle memory takes over.

Example: “Archive Project” placed directly beside “Add Task.”

try.q: “Archive Project” sits right next to “Add Task” with a similar icon. Which problem is this?
options: Bad neighbours
Lack of clarity
Communication failure
Cognitive overload
try.explain: A high-impact action next to a routine one invites mis-clicks.

test.q: What is the order Calabro argues for?
options: Make it work, then make it look good
Make it look good, then test it
Build the design system, then the flows
Ship fast, then fix what users report
test.explain: “We must first make things that work, and then, and only then, make sure they look visually appealing.”

test.q: As an interface gets more stripped-down, what does it need more of?
options: Structure, context and visible rules
White space, larger typography and fewer controls
Animation to explain the layout
Onboarding tours for new users
test.explain: Minimal screens leave users with fewer clues.

test.q: Which is an example of a weak signifier?
options: A button that looks like plain text
An error message in technical language
A modal that covers the table behind it
A delete button next to a save button
test.explain: Users can't tell it is interactive.

test.q: An edit modal covers the table users need to refer to. Which heuristic does this break?
options: Recognition rather than recall
Aesthetic and minimalist design
Flexibility and efficiency of use
Help and documentation
test.explain: It forces users to remember what they were just looking at.

options: Users experience the product, not the design file
Figma is the wrong tool for product teams
Design files should be shared with users before launch
Users dislike modern visual styles
test.explain: Polish in the file doesn't matter if the product doesn't work.
